**This is an AI-generated book.** The manuscript is being revised and independently tested.
No human-authored edition is claimed. Until a lesson has passed a documented
human listening test, treat its code and descriptions of sound as claims that
still need a human ear.

If you have a correction or suggestion, [submit a pull
request](https://github.com/gauden/coding-harmony/pulls). Individual responses may be
limited, but useful corrections can still find their way into the book through
that public record.
:::

Explaining a subject exposes the gaps that private study can leave undisturbed.
That is the method of this book: turn ideas from music theory into Sonic Pi
programs, listen to the result, and examine the places where model and sound
disagree. The website keeps that process visible, including the rough edges that
a finished textbook usually hides.

Sonic Pi is usually introduced as a way to teach programming through music. That
is a useful route, but it moves slowly for someone who already writes software.
Loops and threads receive the attention while harmony, melody, and rhythm wait
offstage. This book starts from the other side: programming is the shared
language, and arrays, functions, state, and concurrency become ways of handling
musical structure.

The 58 lessons are written for a programmer who begins unable to read a note.
They follow the order in which the subject can become concrete. The book begins
with sound itself, then represents pitch and
time as data. Acoustics explains why some relationships recur; rhythm,
intervals, scales, and harmony give those relationships names; notation and
transcription arrive only after there is something familiar to notate. By the
capstones, the short array from the early lessons has grown into named voices
sharing a timeline. The representation grows because the music asks more of it.

## How the lessons work

Each lesson takes one musical idea, finds a representation for it, and plays the
result. You then change one part while the others stay fixed. That small
experiment gives the explanation something concrete to account for: a note
moves, a cadence weakens, or a rhythm shifts its weight. Sonic Pi is the
laboratory, and your programming experience supplies stable ground while the
musical vocabulary develops.

Six decisions shape the course:

- **Sound first, name second.** You meet an interval, cadence, or mode as an
  audible event. Its name arrives when it can help you recognise the event
  again.
- **Music is data.** A reusable event carries `:note`, `:start`, `:duration`, and
  sometimes `:amp`. Later fields describe articulation, spelling, or provenance.
- **Score and renderer stay separate.** The score records content. A playback
  function interprets it. Changing an instrument should not rewrite the notes.
- **Examples end with musical material.** Test tones can isolate a fact, but a
  phrase, groove, or progression reveals what that fact does over time.
- **Notation arrives late.** The staff appears in Part 8, once pitch and duration
  are familiar as numbers. It becomes another coordinate system to decode.
- **Ear work runs beside theory.** From Part 2 onward, short drills ask you to
  recognise each new category without seeing its label. The goal is to make the
  term answer to the sound.

Ruby idioms receive a short explanation when they first appear. The complete
subset used here is collected in [Ruby for
non-Rubyists](appendix/ruby-for-non-rubyists.qmd). Sonic Pi calls are collected
in the [cheat sheet](appendix/sonic-pi-cheatsheet.qmd). Each *Take it further*
exercise has an entry in the [solutions appendix](appendix/solutions.qmd),
including structural checks for exercises whose musical answer remains open.

This is not a course in instrumental technique. It is an account of what
musicians organise and why, expressed in representations you can inspect,
test, revise, and argue with. A program cannot settle every musical question.
It can make the question precise enough to hear.

## Working rhythm

Four sessions a week cover the 58-lesson spine across roughly fifteen weeks,
with the capstones afterward. The schedule below gives new material time to
recur before the next layer arrives.

| Session | Length | What |
|---|---|---|
| Two per week | 25 to 35 min | New lessons, in order. |
| One per week | 30 min | Consolidation. Rebuild one recent example from memory. |
| One per week | 30 min | Free play using only the ideas met so far. |
| Most days | 10 min | Ear drills from your own `drills.rb`. |

Every fourth week, leave new theory alone and reconstruct a short phrase by ear
using only material already introduced. Once Parts 8 and 9 have supplied
notation, source handling, and a transcription workflow, that reconstruction
can grow into a sourced transcription. A concept changes character when a wrong
value keeps a phrase from sounding like its source; it has become a diagnostic
tool rather than a definition to remember.

Run each example in a fresh Sonic Pi buffer unless a comment says that it
continues from above. Read the code once before pressing Run, then listen without
editing. Make the *Change one thing* variations separately; when pitch, timing,
and timbre all move together, the ear has no clean comparison to make. Stop live
loops before moving to the next lesson, since they continue after you change
buffers.

## A word on status

Every lesson carries `status: draft`. The label says that the planned concept,
exercise, explanation, and substantive Ruby example are present, and that the
Ruby clears a syntax check. It says nothing yet about the experience of working
through the lesson in Sonic Pi. Syntax can confirm the shape of a program while
missing an invalid API call, a poor balance, or a misleading description of what
the notes seem to do.

A lesson reaches `tested` only when someone starts cold, follows it in Sonic Pi,
records where it fails, and rewrites from those field notes. Recordings come
after that pass. Until then, timing, synth balance, API behaviour, and every
description of sound await audition. Keeping that distinction visible is part
of the method. Code can parse while the musical result remains wrong.
